title: The Phantom Queries
subtitle: Non-existent records bypass the cache and hammer the primary database

brief.narrative: At 03:00 AM, an unauthorized automated botnet begins probing the SDPD Public Incident Lookup portal. The botnet scripts fire over 3,000 requests per second with random UUIDs and negative integer IDs that do not exist anywhere in the city database. Because these phantom keys do not exist in the Redis cache, every single request registers as a Cache Miss. The application servers dutifully query the primary PostgreSQL database to fetch the missing records. The database engine executes millions of futile index lookups and table scans trying to find non-existent rows. Within minutes, database CPU hits 100%, disk read IOPS are completely saturated, and all 150 connection pool slots are locked up. Real field detectives running emergency suspect lookups are hit with 504 Gateway Timeouts. The cache sits virtually untouched with low memory usage while the database underneath is crushed.
symptoms: Primary database CPU sustained at 100% with connection pool exhaustion (150/150 connections busy)
Redis cache hit ratio plummeted from 94% to under 6%
Field detectives reporting 504 Gateway Timeouts on critical warrant and suspect lookups
API access logs reveal millions of queries for non-existent IDs like -9999 and random hashes
brief.objective: Diagnose why non-existent keys bypass cache protection, and implement a strategy to filter out invalid queries before they reach the database.

rootCause.question: What is the root cause of the system failure under the botnet queries?

options.text: Cache Penetration: The botnet is querying IDs that do not exist, completely bypassing Redis cache hits and routing thousands of futile queries directly into the primary database
options.feedback: Correct! This is the classic Cache Penetration problem. When queries target keys that exist neither in the cache nor in the database, every request is a cache miss that hits the database. Because the database returns nothing, the cache is never populated with an answer, so subsequent queries for the same invalid keys hit the database again and again until the database connection pool collapses.

options.text: Cache Eviction: Redis has run out of memory and is aggressively evicting incident records under its LRU policy
options.feedback: Inspection of Redis shows it is only using 12.4 GB out of 64 GB available (under 20%), with zero evictions. Redis is completely healthy and has plenty of RAM; the issue is that the requested keys simply never existed.

options.text: Index Corruption: The incident ID column on the PostgreSQL database has lost its index, causing full sequential table scans
options.feedback: The database logs confirm B-tree index scans are active. The problem is that searching an index 3,000 times per second for non-existent keys across millions of rows still consumes massive disk IOPS and CPU.

options.text: Network Partition: A split-brain network failure has severed communication between the API gateway and the Redis cluster
options.feedback: The API is communicating with Redis without any network drops. Redis is responding with key misses in under 1ms; the problem is that the application forwards every miss to the database.

fix.question: How should the architecture be updated to protect the database against cache penetration?

options.text: Implement a Bloom Filter before the database to reject non-existent IDs with zero DB queries, and cache empty/null results with a short TTL
options.feedback: Correct! A Bloom filter is an extremely fast, space-efficient probabilistic data structure that can tell you if an ID definitely does NOT exist. If the Bloom filter says no, the request is rejected immediately without touching Redis or PostgreSQL. For borderline cases, caching null values with a short TTL (e.g., 60s) ensures repeated lookups for recently queried missing keys are absorbed by Redis rather than hitting the database.

options.text: Scale Redis horizontally by adding 10 replica nodes to increase read throughput
options.feedback: Adding Redis replicas will not help. Redis is already handling the traffic easily at 15% CPU. The problem is that Redis does not have the keys, so adding more replicas just means more nodes reporting cache misses.

options.text: Increase the PostgreSQL database connection pool from 150 to 3,000 connections
options.feedback: Increasing the connection pool will make the problem worse. 3,000 concurrent database queries will cause catastrophic CPU context-switching and thrash disk IOPS even harder, leading to kernel panic.

options.text: Configure the API Gateway to return HTTP 200 with mock incident data whenever a query times out
options.feedback: Returning fake mock data to police officers during active suspect investigations creates severe legal liabilities and safety hazards, while leaving the underlying database overload completely unaddressed.
